No functional, behavioural, or code-level quality measure (e.g. HTML validity, semantic structure, maintainability, responsiveness) — based on metric definitions pp. 3–4. For our project this means Design2Code says nothing about whether a rebuilt page works or is maintainable.
587	- [I] JavaScript, iframes, SVG and external links are stripped and prompts say no JS is needed (pp. 13–14); the task is reconstruction of a static, de-functionalised snapshot, not of an application.
588	- [I] Human validation is modest: 100 pages, Fleiss' κ only 0.46/0.32/0.26 (p. 16), logistic regression accuracy 79.9% on a 50-page test half (p. 7). The very high Pearson r = 0.975 is computed over only 10 system-level points (p. 17) and compares predicted wins with human "win + tie" — an aggregation that inflates agreement.
589	- [I] Test pages come from C4, a common pretraining corpus; data contamination is not discussed (grep for "contamin" finds nothing).
590	- [I] Single run per configuration with greedy decoding; no variance or significance testing between models (pp. 5–6, 14).
591	- [I] Design2Code-HARD pages are sourced from GitHub (p. 14) and filtered "using the same filtering process" (p. 8); how the GitHub pages were found and selected is not described, so the HARD set's representativeness cannot be judged.
592	- [I] The metric-validation agreement is not out-of-sample. The logistic regression is trained on 50 of the 100 human-annotated pages (p. 7); the linear model for simulated win rates is refit "on the same training examples" and applied to "all 484 examples", which include those training pages (p. 17); and the human "win + tie" rates it is compared with come from the same 100 pages (Table 8, p. 17). So r = 0.975 / τ = 0.931 partly reflects fit on the training data, on top of being computed over only 10 system-level points.
593	- [I] Element metrics are text-anchored (blocks come from text segments, p. 13); images, icons and non-text elements are only covered by CLIP.

20	## 9. Limitations we identified
21	- [I] **IFS and VFS are not comparable in scale.** VFS averages only over checkpoints that were "successfully reached" (p. 7). It therefore cannot be lowered by functional failures that block later states. IFS divides successful actions by all actions in the trajectory (p. 7). Part of the IFS < VFS gap is therefore a property of the metrics, not only of the models. The authors mention unreachable states only to justify alpha = 0.7 (p. 7). How VFS is scored for a task where no visual checkpoint is reached is not reported. This weakens the headline "visual is solved better than function" reading. It does not weaken the finding that IFS is low in absolute terms.
22	- [I] **No code-quality or maintainability measurement.** The task forces a single self-contained HTML file with no libraries (p. 20), and only behaviour and appearance are scored. The benchmark therefore says nothing about code structure, readability or maintainability (our RQ3), and the single-file format is far from how real apps are built.
23	- [I] **Judge overlap.** Gemini-2.5-Pro is both the assertion/visual judge (p. 7) and one of the evaluated models (p. 8). Self-preference bias is not tested; its mid-table rank makes a large bias unlikely, but it is not ruled out.
24	- [I] **Moderate human alignment, tuned in-sample.** The weights were chosen to maximise rho on the same 60 instances used to report rho = 0.57 / 0.65 (p. 17); there is no held-out check. These are moderate correlations, so the Final Score is only partly aligned with human judgement. Agreement among the five raters is not reported (p. 17). The same is true of agreement among the three PhD students who observed the agent (p. 9).
25	- [I] **Evaluator re-scoring after fixes unclear.** The 3/100 agent failures were "rectified" (p. 9). Whether all 28 x 113 evaluations were re-run after the fixes is not reported. Element resolution from natural-language descriptions (p. 17) may itself involve a model, so the "deterministic" label (p. 6) is an author claim we cannot check.
26	- [I] **No variance reporting.** Single point estimates with default sampling settings (p. 8) and no repeated runs reported; several model gaps are tiny (e.g. 30.36 vs 30.31, p. 9) and could be noise.
27	- [I] **Unclear failure propagation.** It is not stated whether a failed early action stops the replay or whether later actions are still attempted (p. 7); Case 4 suggests failures cascade (p. 21). This affects how IFS should be read.
28	- [I] **Possible contamination.** Tasks come from popular live websites (e.g. an IMDb mock in Figure 2, p. 2); models may have seen similar code in training. Asset anonymisation (p. 5) reduces name cues but not memorised page structure. Not discussed by the authors.
29	- [I] **Small strata.** L1 (about 9 tasks) and L4 (about 12 tasks), derived by us from the percentages on p. 3, give unstable per-category scores.
30	## 10. Threats to validity
31	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Task filtering removed "overly trivial" and "disputed" tasks without stated criteria (p. 6), which may shift difficulty. All models get identical inputs and prompt (p. 18), which supports a fair comparison. Video downsampling to at most 64 frames (p. 8) may remove interaction evidence from long videos (max 172.9 s, p. 6); this affects all models equally but penalises long tasks.
32	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] Front-end only, one HTML file, mocked backend (p. 20); 113 tasks. Results do not transfer directly to multi-file apps, backends, or native desktop/mobile apps.
33	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] IFS measures replay of one ground-truth trajectory, not general behavioural equivalence; VFS mixes OCR, DINO and an MLLM rubric in which text content carries 40 of 100 points (p. 20). Both are proxies for "functional fidelity" and "visual fidelity". They also use different denominators: VFS covers only reached checkpoints, IFS all actions (p. 7). So the size of the IFS-VFS gap is partly metric-induced and should not be read as a direct comparison of the two capabilities. The fixed alpha = 0.7 encodes a value judgement (functionality matters more), supported only by rho = 0.65 (p. 17).
34	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs, tests or repeated runs (p. 8-9); conclusions about small differences (thinking vs non-thinking) are not statistically supported.
35	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Prompts are published in the appendix (p. 20-21) and data and code are promised (p. 1). Proprietary model versions, default sampling settings and a proprietary judge model (p. 7) limit exact reproduction.

[I] Each stage is probably an independent generation, not an evolution of the previous codebase, because the four stage prompts are self-contained (p. 5).
912	- Sampling / selection method: 90 problems "randomly sampled" (p. 4), later described as a "stratified sample" balanced across Easy/Medium/Hard (p. 9) [V]. Model selection to span dense vs MoE, proprietary vs open, and parameter scale [V] (p. 3).
913	- Data availability (public? link?): replication package at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19245562 with sampling scripts, Exp I scripts, Exp II prompts and analysis scripts [V] (p. 10). Generated repositories announced as a benchmark dataset "released alongside this paper" [A] (p. 5).
914	## 5. Experimental setup
915	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: each solution saved as a .py file and analysed with PyExamine; counts per smell type aggregated [V] (p. 4). Exp II repositories also measured with cloc (TLoC), total number of files (ToF) and Agent Action Count (AAC) [V] (p. 5). No iterative "validate and correct" loop in Exp I (budget) [V] (p. 9). Temperature, sampling settings, model quantisation/hosting, PyExamine version and thresholds: not reported. Results for AAC: not reported. The factor "ALpF" in Table 3 is not defined in the text (p. 9).
916	- Code availability: scripts in the Zenodo package (p. 10).
917	## 6. Evaluation metrics
918	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
919	  - PyExamine smell counts at three levels: code-level (e.g. Long Method, Long File, High Cyclomatic Complexity), structural (class/object level, e.g. Too Many Branches, High Response for a Class, Temporal Field) and architectural (e.g. Unstable Dependency, Scattered Functionality, Potential Improper API Usage) [V] (p. 3, p. 7, p. 8). Chosen as a comprehensive, "un-opinionated", static and repeatable Python smell detector, and to separate structural smells from superficial linting issues counted by SonarQube [A] (p. 2, p. 4).
920	  - TLoC and ToF as project size/complexity [V] (p. 5).
921	  - Feature Envy and Potential Shotgun Surgery were excluded from Exp I interpretation after a manual audit found systematic false positives; Long Method and Long File were judged high precision [V] (p. 6). The size of this audit and precision values are not reported.
922	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Exp I — raw counts only, no statistical test, no normalisation by code size [V] (p. 7). Exp II — Spearman's ρ (continuous factors) and Kruskal-Wallis H (Scenario, Stage), p < 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction, no confidence intervals [V] (p. 8, p. 9). Functional correctness of generated code: not measured or reported.
923	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
924	- [A] No iterative debug/repair loop in Exp I; first-pass code only (p. 9, p. 10).
925	- [A] Exp I uses 90 problems, not the full dataset; may miss long-tail problem types; authors plan to scale up "to verify the statistical significance of these findings" (p. 9).
926	- [A] Exp II uses only MetaGPT; findings may be specific to its SOP-based paradigm; other tools (SpecKit, Cursor Composer) may differ (p. 9, p. 10).
927	- [A] Small sample, so non-parametric tests were used (p. 8).
928	## 9. Limitations we identified
929	- [I] Central claims rest on very small counts. Exp I differences are a handful of smell instances over 90 files (e.g. 11 vs 1 Long Method), with no test, no per-LoC normalisation and no variance across runs (p. 7). Treat as descriptive.
930	- [I] The "Volume-Quality Inverse Law" correlates smell *counts* with code size (p. 8, p. 9). More code mechanically yields more smell instances, so ρ = 0.94 does not show that larger code is worse per line. The paper says size metrics allow density normalisation (p. 5) but reports no density analysis.
931	- [I] The claims that functional correctness does not mitigate decay (p. 1, p. 2) are not backed by any reported correctness measure; Exp II apps were not executed or tested at all as far as the paper reports.
932	- [I] The "longitudinal"/"architectural rot" framing (p. 2, p. 5) is questionable: the four stage prompts are self-contained (p. 5), and the paper does not say that each stage evolves the previous codebase. It may be four independent generations.
933	- [I] Exp II has n ≈ 20, one LLM backend, one framework, no human or single-agent baseline, and 15 significance tests without correction (p. 9); the "near-perfect predictor" wording overstates a single small sample.
934	- [I] Internal inconsistencies: RQ numbering differs between introduction and results; "random" vs "stratified" sampling; "ALpF" undefined; smell abbreviations in Exp I (EC, HFI) are not expanded (p. 1, p. 4, p. 6, p. 7, p. 9).
935	- [I] PyExamine validity: two smell types were dropped as false positives after an unquantified audit (p. 6); no precision figures for the architectural smells that drive the main conclusion.
936	- [I] Model inference settings (temperature, quantisation; model names suggest local deployment) are not reported, which limits reproducibility.
937	## 10. Threats to validity
938	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): size confounds smell counts (Exp II); CodeContests problems may be in model training data (not discussed); prompts for Exp II were engineered to force modularity after preliminary trials (p. 5).
939	- External (generalisability of sample/context): Python only; competitive programming tasks (Exp I); five small app scenarios with a single agent framework and one LLM (Exp II) (p. 5, p. 9, p. 10).
940	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): maintainability is equated with PyExamine smell counts; no human assessment of maintainability; FE and PSS judged unreliable (p. 6).
941	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no tests in Exp I; small n and no correction in Exp II; no repeated generations, so model randomness is not estimated (p. 7, p. 8, p. 9).
942	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): Zenodo package with scripts and prompts (p. 10); generation hyper-parameters not reported. Authors note Gemini 3.1 was used for editorial purposes (p. 10).
943	## 12. Relevance to our research
944	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (main), RQ1, RQ4.
945	- How it informs our work [I]: Exp II is close to our setting: complete small applications (games, GUI tools, web backend) generated by an agent from natural-language requirements. It gives a smell taxonomy for agent-built apps (God-class branching, unstable dependencies, scattered functionality) that a reconstruction study could measure. Its evidence is weak (preprint version, tiny n, count-based statistics, no correctness data), so it should support hypotheses rather than conclusions, and it illustrates RQ4 weaknesses (no size normalisation, no baselines).

content.content:
######## liu2026benchmarking
## 7. Key findings
1. Best effectiveness: GPT-Engineer + Claude-Haiku 4.5, Req.Acc 53.75 ± 0.43, Test.Acc 69.41 ± 1.07 (p. 6, Table 3). [V] Excluding MetaGPT, all Claude-Haiku 4.5, GPT-4o and Qwen-Max settings fall between 42.30 and 53.75 Req.Acc (p. 6). [V] The authors summarise: "achieving only 30%–50% Req. Acc." and no model exceeds 60% (p. 5). [A]
2. Soft Req.Acc exceeds Req.Acc by about 25–33 points in most settings (e.g. GPT-Engineer + Claude-Haiku 4.5: 0.5402 vs 0.7991), meaning partially working requirements are common (p. 25, Table 10). [V] Table 10's strict Req.Acc (0.5402) differs from the Table 3 value for the same setting (53.75, p. 6); see §9. The authors attribute this to failing edge cases and fine details (p. 6). [A]
3. Agentic frameworks do not reliably beat a plain prompted LLM: e.g. GPT-4o-mini Vanilla 44.82 Req.Acc vs ChatDev 33.16 and MapCoder 41.30; GPT-4o Vanilla 45.95 vs ChatDev 42.71 (p. 6, Table 3). [V] Cost (Table 3, p. 6) [V]: most multi-agent frameworks (MapCoder, ChatDev, MetaGPT) cost several times more than Vanilla, but the absolute costs are small:
   - GPT-4o ChatDev costs $0.1947 vs Vanilla $0.0160, about 12x.
   - Claude-Haiku 4.5 ChatDev costs $0.174 vs $0.015, about 11.6x.
   - On Qwen-7B, ChatDev costs $0.0075 vs $0.0003 (about 25x) and MetaGPT $0.0207 vs $0.0003 (about 69x). The Vanilla cost is rounded to 4 decimals, so these two ratios are imprecise.

   Self-Collaboration, also a multi-agent framework (p. 5), costs about the same as Vanilla (Claude-Haiku 4.5 $0.014 vs $0.015; GPT-4o $0.0155 vs $0.0160) (p. 6). The paper itself states no cost ratio; the ratios above are our arithmetic on Table 3 [I]. All four multi-agent frameworks take longer than Vanilla on every backbone, e.g. GPT-4o: Vanilla 28 s; Self-Collaboration 37 s; MapCoder 93 s; ChatDev 114 s; MetaGPT 66 s (p. 6). [V]
4. MetaGPT almost completely fails (0.00–5.39 Req.Acc), attributed to inter-agent communication breakdowns: 44% of its failures are code inconsistency (missing files, syntax errors) (p. 6, p. 8). [V]/[A]
5. The same frameworks reach 71–91% Pass@1 on HumanEval (except MetaGPT), far above their E2EDev scores (p. 27, Table 12). [V]
6. OpenHands and SWE-Agent underperform the Vanilla baseline (Claude-Haiku 4.5: 43.45 and 44.73 vs 48.69 Req.Acc) (p. 23, Table 8). [V] The authors explain this by task mismatch with their original design (p. 22). [A]
7. Human failure analysis of 360 projects: four failure types (code inconsistency, requirement missing, requirement misaligned, detail mismatch); Vanilla LLM and ChatDev show the most missing requirements; Vanilla shows the fewest detail mismatches (p. 7–8, p. 23). [V]/[A]
8. The semi-automated pipeline needed human refinement for ~20% of requirements, ~50% of test cases and <20% of test scripts, at ~3.5 hours and ~$0.48 GPT-4o cost per project (p. 15–17). [V]

######## pan2026functional
## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Functional correctness is low. The average functional score is 33.98% for standard and 30.23% for thinking LLMs, and no model exceeds 45%. Best: Gemini-3-Pro-Preview 43.86% and Gemini-2.5-Pro-Thinking 43.44%; lowest: DeepSeek-R1 16.23% (p. 5; p. 6).
2. [V] Non-functional averages are higher: 52.25% for standard and 49.57% for thinking LLMs. For standard LLMs, average maintainability is 33.45% and security 87.40% (p. 5; p. 6).
3. [V] NF separates models that functional scores do not: Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-4o have almost equal functional scores (27.63% vs 27.48%) but NF of 35.15% vs 57.59% (p. 5).
4. [V] Thinking models are not consistently better and on average score slightly below standard LLMs (p. 6).
5. [V] Failure taxonomy: requirement–implementation mismatches plus non-functional quality failures make up 82.8% of failures; executability/dependency failures make up 17.2% (p. 7).
6. [V] Cost per run ranges from $0.15 (DeepSeek-V3.2) to $16.63 (Claude-3.7-Sonnet-Thinking), averaging $4.10 for standard and $11.00 for thinking models. Higher cost does not reliably buy a higher functional score (p. 8).
7. [V] On GPT-5.2, none of the three one-shot strategies beat the baseline (41.80% functional, 57.10% NF). S1 scored 37.70/46.10, S2 40.20/49.90 and S3 41.20/49.60; all three lowered NF (p. 8; p. 9).
8. [V] Prompt variants moved GPT-5.2's mean functional score from 0.4181 (baseline) to 0.4972 (clarified) and 0.4919 (paraphrased). The authors call the differences small (p. 9).
9. [V] Functional scores had Std = 0 and CV = 0 across 5 reruns for all three models and all 38 projects; the median NF CV was 0.0007 (p. 6; p. 7).
10. [V] The NF model ranking is stable under equal weights, uncapped normalisation and leave-one-out variants (Spearman 0.90–0.99), but not under a rank-based aggregate (0.6441) (p. 10).
11. [V] Defect-injection sanity check: the functional suites detected all 76 injected defects (2 per task); the robustness suites detected 0.375 of them (p. 5).

######## tran2026vibe
## 7. Key findings
1. Top test-split accuracy: GPT-5.3-Codex 61.77 ± 4.71%, Claude Opus 4.6 57.57 ± 4.37%, GPT-5.2 53.50 ± 5.07%; lowest Grok 4.1 Fast Reasoning 1.20 ± 1.20% (p. 6, Table 4). [V] Open-weight models range ~5–23% (p. 6, Table 4). [V]
2. Accuracy falls with difficulty (all-model average 44.29% easy, 21.36% medium, 6.03% hard) and with external integrations (34.18% none vs 13.49% email + Stripe) (p. 6, Tables 5–6). [V] Average by domain: Individual 43.01%, Solo Founder 29.94%, Enterprise Tool 18.64% (p. 7, Table 7). [V]
3. Browser tool calls per app correlate with accuracy across the 16 models (Pearson r = 0.72; partial r = 0.72 controlling for latency); edit calls barely correlate (r = 0.09) (p. 7). [V] The authors interpret this as self-testing being associated with better outcomes (p. 7). [A]
4. Failures are mostly zero-score apps: 12.8% of apps score zero for the top five models vs 73.2% for the bottom five; 14.0% of apps from the worst five fail to start; only 8.8% of top-five apps score 100% (p. 7). [V]
5. Behavioural failure taxonomy (apps that started): missing feature 46.7%, authorization 20.4%, validation/policy block 14.8%, UI rendering/navigation 6.0%, data consistency/backend 1.9%, other 10.2% (p. 8). [V] How failures were classified (human or LLM) is not reported.
6. Variance: generation-side variance dominates (92.5%, 92.1%, 73.5% of observed variance for Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6); evaluator rerun SE 0.99–3.00 pp vs generation SE 3.47–5.00 pp (p. 8, Table 9). [V] The authors conclude rankings are robust except for near-ties (p. 8). [A]
7. Human–human step agreement 88.6–93.6%; Claude Sonnet 4.5 (canonical evaluator) 86.4% mean agreement with humans, Claude Sonnet 4.6 86.3%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 84.7%, GPT-5.2 only 36.1% (p. 9, Table 10). [V] Model–model agreement ranges 33.1–87.8% (p. 9). [V]
8. Vibe Code Bench separates models more than SWE-Bench: MiniMax M2.5 vs Claude Opus 4.6 gap 2.8% on SWE-Bench vs 42.7% on VCB (p. 2). [V] (57.57 − 14.85 = 42.72, consistent with Table 4.)

######## wu2026looks
## 7. Key findings
1. Build success is 100% for all six models; authors attribute this to the harness's verify-repair loop, not the model [V] (pp. 6–7, 12).
2. NavPassRate: Opus 4.6 92%, GPT-5 89%, Haiku 4.5 85%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 82%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 62%, GPT-5 Mini 58% [V] (p. 7).
3. Visual fidelity has not saturated: Borda 0.906 (Opus) to 0.130 (GPT-5 Mini); point-wise means 1.60–2.99/5, so even the best model stays below 3/5; Opus leads in 26 of 29 apps [V] (pp. 6–7). The gap is concentrated in cross-page Consistency: models re-implement navigation chrome inline per page instead of sharing a component [A] (p. 6).
4. Maintainability is dissociated from visual fidelity: Opus writes 1,441 LoC (82 LoC/file) vs GPT-5 668 (33 LoC/file); GPT-5 has higher reuse (4.23 vs 3.83) and fewer dead components (7.8% vs 19.9%); ColorConsistency saturates at 0.74–0.85 [V] (pp. 6–7). Authors: "maintainability is uncorrelated with visual fidelity" [A] (p. 8) — no correlation coefficient is computed.
5. Cost: $0.15 (GPT-5 Mini) to $2.90 (Opus) per app; GPT-5 ($0.50, Borda 0.542, NavPass 89%) dominates Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on cost and quality [V] (p. 7). Cheaper models fabricate content (Lorem ipsum, stock imagery) [A] (p. 7).
6. Navigation failure taxonomy (n = 64 stratified hand-labelled failures from 3,486 executions): C1 blank starting page 7.8% [3.0, 18.3]; C2 route mapping error 10.9% [5.4, 20.9]; C3 target unreachable/occluded 32.8% [22.6, 45.0]; C4 click has no effect 48.4% [36.6, 60.4] [V] (p. 8). C4 (missing or mis-wired onClick) dominates for Opus and GPT-5 (75% of their labelled failures); C3 for GPT-5 Mini (67%); C1 for Gemini 2.5 Flash (42%) [V] (pp. 8, 15). Build checks do not catch silent event-handler bugs [A] (p. 8).
7. Per-app difficulty varies widely: point-wise visual 3.62 (Notion) to 2.01 (Apple News); NavPass 0.45 (Medium) to 1.00 (Khan Academy) [V] (pp. 7, 12).

######## zhou2025declarui
## 7. Key findings
1. React Native: DeclarUI (Claude-3.5) CLIP 0.88, SSIM 0.68, PCR 96.8%, CSR 98%; DeclarUI (GPT-4o) 0.87 / 0.58 / 88.6% / 88%; baselines GPT-4o 0.66 / 0.44 / 1.4% / 76% and Claude-3.5 0.65 / 0.41 / 43.3% / 74% [V] (p. 9).
2. Raw MLLMs largely fail to implement multi-page navigation (GPT-4o PCR 1.4%) [V] (p. 9). Baseline compilation failures came from non-existent packages/components, special-character handling and missing imports [A] (p. 8).
3. Generalisation: Flutter PCR 99.4%, CSR 92%; ArkUI PCR 95.9%, CSR 86% (DeclarUI Claude-3.5 only) [V] (p. 9). Knowledge-graph RAG for ArkUI on 20 apps: CSR 86% → 90%, AMCT 183 s → 43.5 s [V] (p. 11).
4. Ablation (13 apps): removing CV extraction drops SSIM 0.72 → 0.57; removing PTG + refinement drops PCR to 23.1% and CSR to 80% [V] (pp. 9–10).
5. User study (5 developers × 12 apps): DeclarUI vs Baseline (Claude-3.5) — availability 4.97 vs 4.15, modification time 4.03 vs 2.45, readability 4.62 vs 3.75, maintainability 4.55 vs 3.37, all p < 0.05 (Mann-Whitney U) [V] (p. 10). 73.3% of DeclarUI code modified within 10 min; 80% of baseline code needed >10 min [V] (p. 10).
6. Manual repair: AMCT 48 s (React Native, Claude-3.5), 43.2 s (GPT-4o), 62 s (Flutter), 183 s (ArkUI) [V] (p. 11).
7. Authors conclude generated code "meets industrial-grade standards" in availability, modification time, readability and maintainability [A] (pp. 1–2) — this rests on Likert ratings from five developers.

######## zhu2026understanding
## 7. Key findings
1. Exp I: Long Method counts were higher for larger LLMs than for humans — zero-shot Qwen Coder 480B 11, Qwen Coder 30B 7, Gemini 2.5 Pro 5, deepseek 2, Llama 3 70B 0, human 1 (across 90 problems) — [V] (p. 7, Table 1).
2. Exp I: Temporal Field appeared only in human solutions (4 instances), never in LLM output — [V] (p. 6, p. 7).
3. Exp I: few-shot prompting did not reduce Long Method (Qwen 480B 11 → 13; Gemini 5 → 8) — [V] (p. 6, p. 7, Table 2).
4. Exp I interpretation: a "Reasoning-Complexity Trade-off" — more capable models produce more procedural bloat; larger models' failed solutions had more Long Methods — [A] (p. 6, p. 7). The failed/passing split is not shown in any table.
5. Exp II: ranked by mean count over all Exp II repositories (pooled), the most prevalent smells were Too Many Branches, High Response for a Class, Potential Improper API Usage, Scattered Functionality and Unstable Dependency — [V] (p. 8, Figure 1 caption; p. 7). The authors add that these smells appear consistently "across all stages and scenarios" — [A] (p. 7); Figure 1 pools repositories and no per-stage or per-scenario breakdown is shown.
6. Exp II: TLoC correlated with code-level (ρ = 0.53, p = 0.017), structural (ρ = 0.59, p = 0.007) and architectural smell counts (ρ = 0.94, p < 0.001); ToF with architectural smells ρ = 0.72 (p < 0.001) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9, Table 3).
7. Exp II: scenario affected architectural smells (H = 9.86, p = 0.043); requirement stage had no significant effect on any smell level (p > 0.8) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9, Table 3).
8. Authors' framing: a "Volume-Quality Inverse Law" and a "Modular Mirage" (files are separated but behaviour is fragmented); agents act like "junior developers" lacking architectural foresight — [A] (p. 8, p. 9).
9. Abstract/introduction claim that functional correctness is decoupled from quality ("running code is just as likely to be structurally flawed as failed code") — [A] (p. 1, p. 2). No supporting data is reported in the results.

######## molison2025llm
## 7. Key findings
1. [V] SonarQube found no security vulnerabilities in any dataset (p. 5).
2. [V] Odds of a SonarQube bug in LLM solutions vs human solutions were very low in every configuration and level: zero-shot 0.008 / 0.006 / 0.0005, few-shot 0.003 / 0.006 / 0.001, fine-tuned 0.00 / 0.019 / 0.0005 (introductory / interview / competition), all p < 0.001 (Table II, p. 8).
3. [V] Code smells were mixed: zero-shot had 3.57× the odds of a smell vs human for introductory problems (p < 0.001); few-shot vs human was 0.52 for competition (p < 0.05); fine-tuned vs human was 0.00 for introductory and competition (p < 0.001); several other comparisons were not significant (Table III, p. 8).
4. [V] In the human dataset, bug-type issues were dominated by Blocker severity (87.50% introductory, 71.27% interview, 86.30% competition, Table I) (p. 8). [A] The authors interpret these as "bug rates" (p. 6).
5. [V] Average SonarQube effort to fix (min): introductory human 7.20, zero-shot 3.75, few-shot 4.72, fine-tuned 5.00; interview human 7.06, zero-shot 5.48, few-shot 6.13, fine-tuned 4.67; competition human 6.95, zero-shot 6.14, few-shot 7.33, fine-tuned 7.60 (Fig. 6, p. 7). [A] "LLMs reduced effort in simpler tasks, but this advantage diminished as the tasks became more complex" (p. 7).
6. [V] Cliff's delta for effort, zero-shot vs human: 0.54 large (introductory), 0.21 small (interview), 0.1 negligible (competition), all significant; fine-tuned vs human introductory 0.24 small and fine-tuned vs zero-shot introductory −0.50 large are not marked significant (Table IV, p. 8).
7. [V] Severity shift: for interview problems fine-tuning had 94.1% minor, 2.1% major, 1.2% critical, 2.6% blocker issues, vs human 10.7% blocker (p. 6). For competition problems the human dataset had the fewest critical issues relative to LLM outputs (p. 6). [A] LLMs "may introduce more critical issues compared to human-generated code" on competition tasks (Finding 3, p. 6).
8. [V] Pass@1 on 15 sampled solutions per approach: human 1.0, zero-shot 0.53, few-shot 0.87, fine-tuned 0.47 (Table V, p. 8). Partial (some test cases passed) solutions: 47% of zero-shot, 13% of few-shot and fine-tuned (p. 8). Failures included runtime errors, wrong outputs, hard-coded inputs, waiting for input indefinitely and syntax errors (p. 8).
9. [A] The fine-tuned model has "the best quality metrics" yet "struggled to generate code for complex solutions" (p. 8); the authors attribute its low performance to too few fine-tuning samples (p. 9).
10. [A] AI models "may better avoid functional bugs than address structural code quality concerns" (p. 9).

<!-- TABLE -->

## Contradictions
<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). -->

Each entry records both sides with page refs, then compares data, population, method, metric and time. Explanations are labelled [I]. We do not pick a side.

### C1. Does AI assistance harm maintainability? he2026speed vs borg2026echoes
- **Side A** [V]: Cursor adoption in 806 OSS repositories raised total SonarQube static-analysis warnings by +30.26% and total cognitive complexity by +41.64% relative to matched controls (Borusyak DiD) [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The complexity effect stays significant after controlling for codebase size in the GMM (0.086, p<0.01) [@he2026speed, p. 8].
- **Side B** [V]: When a second developer evolved AI-co-developed code without AI, there was no significant difference in completion time [@borg2026echoes, p. 33], CodeHealth (8.49 vs 8.44) [@borg2026echoes, p. 38] or test coverage [@borg2026echoes, p. 35]. The only "significant" maintainability effect, a Bayesian +0.10 CodeHealth for code from habitual AI users, favours AI [@borg2026echoes, p. 39].
- **Differences**:
  - Data and population: real-world OSS repositories with ≥10 stars [@he2026speed, p. 4] vs one 2 KLoC Java/Spring Boot task done by 151 volunteer professionals [@borg2026echoes, p. 19; @borg2026echoes, p. 64].
  - Tool generation: an agentic IDE (Cursor Composer/agent) [@he2026speed, p. 2] vs late-2024 assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor) [@borg2026echoes, p. 3; @borg2026echoes, p. 60].
  - Metric: repository-total warnings and cognitive complexity, which scale with code size [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a LoC-weighted file-level CodeHealth average plus a second developer's evolution time [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
  - Time: monthly panel of up to about 20 months [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a single hand-off task.
  - Robustness: he2026speed's quality effects turn negative and non-significant under the Callaway–Sant'Anna estimator (warnings −10.49%, complexity −3.80%) [@he2026speed, p. 16]. borg2026echoes is underpowered (75 of 128 planned participants; 80% power only for d≈0.66) [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
- **Partial agreement** [V]: borg2026echoes' observational Phase 1 also found more duplication (23% vs 11%), more complex conditionals and very large code-volume outliers in AI-assisted code [@borg2026echoes, p. 30; @borg2026echoes, p. 46]. With size controlled, he2026speed finds no direct Cursor effect on warnings [@he2026speed, p. 8].
- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two results need not conflict. Both fit "AI adds more code, and project-level totals rise with it, while per-file health and the short-term effort of the next developer are not clearly worse". The he2026speed effect depends on the estimator, and borg2026echoes can rule out only large effects. Neither study settles the question.

### C2. Fewer or more static-analysis issues in LLM code? molison2025llm vs he2026speed

### C7. Security of generated code: pan2026functional vs zhao2025vibe

### C8. More code or less code? Rebuilds are smaller, but assisted development adds code
- **Side A** [V]: Reconstructions are much smaller than their references. ### C9. Apparent disagreements that come from different constructs (do not pool)

- **G-A1. Whole-application functional fidelity is far from complete** [V]. Every benchmark agrees:
  - Full behavioural equivalence: 2.8% of apps [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] and 0 of 200 programs [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
  - Best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates: 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6].
  - Lower still in some benchmarks: IFS <25 [@chen2025iwr, p. 8], <45% [@pan2026functional, p. 5], 27.8% [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The direction is consistent across 8 independent benchmarks, but 5 of them are preprints and most use single runs.
- **G-A2. Behaviour and interaction are harder than static structure** [V]:
  - Structure beats actions [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
  - Static tasks score higher than interactive ones [@chen2025iwr, p. 16].
  - Interactive parts score lower than full pages [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
  - UI plus logic is harder than logic alone [@kim2026programdistill, p. 38].
  - "Click has no effect" is the largest navigation failure category (48.4%) [@wu2026looks, p. 8].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**, with the measurement caveat in C5.
- **G-A3. Fidelity falls as dependency depth, size or complexity rise** [V]: [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @tran2026vibe, p. 6; @zhao2025vibe, p. 14]. Strength [I]: **moderate**.
- **G-A4. Functional correctness and other quality dimensions diverge** [V]:
  - Best static quality but lowest Pass@1 [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
  - Correct but insecure [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
  - Equal functional scores but very different non-functional scores [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
  - The visual leader is not the maintainability leader [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
  - Authors state that passing functional tests does not imply maintainable code [A] [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The pattern is consistent, but each study measures a different second dimension.
- **G-A5. Rebuilt code is structurally simpler and more monolithic than the original** [V]: [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on 2 preprints, selected subsets and size proxies only.
- **G-A6. Code quality and maintainability are rarely measured in fidelity benchmarks**:
  - Not measured at all [V]: [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5; @kim2026programdistill, p. 14].
  - Explicitly left out [A]: [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
  - Measured only by proxies [V]: size and structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], LoC/reuse proxies [@wu2026looks, p. 4], a single MI index [@pan2026functional, p. 3], Likert ratings [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
  - Strength [I]: **strong** as a description of the field (verified absences across 12+ papers).
- **G-A7. LLM judges must be validated per judge model** [V]:
  - Judge–human agreement ranges from 36.1% to 86.4% depending on the evaluator model [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
  - 86–94% raw agreement on 3 settings [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
  - τ = 0.716 on 55 author-labelled scenarios [@wu2026looks, p. 13].
  - ρ = 0.65, tuned in-sample [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].
  - Low human inter-annotator κ (0.26–0.46) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 16].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**.
- **G-A8. Practitioners perceive vibe-coded output as fast but flawed** [V]: [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8]. This converges with LLM-linked code and design debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16] and with higher review burden for novice agent users [@asdaque2026novice, p. 3]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on perception and proxy evidence, not code measurement.

The broader claim "visual fidelity systematically exceeds functional fidelity" is not supported, because the visual and functional scales are not commensurable across or within papers.

### C6. Multi-agent / agentic frameworks: MetaGPT fails in liu2026benchmarking but leads in mock2026vibe
- **Side A** [V]: MetaGPT nearly always fails on E2EDev (0–5.4% Req.Acc) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6]. Multi-agent frameworks "do not consistently improve" over a plain LLM (by our count, 9 of 24 cells higher [I]) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
- **Side B** [V]: Agentic MetaGPT X runs had the highest test pass rate (mean 94.58%) [@mock2026vibe, p. 25; @mock2026vibe, p. 41]. zhu2026understanding generated complete multi-file apps with MetaGPT, but only after adding explicit modularity prompts [@zhu2026understanding, p. 5].
- **Differences**:
  - Task size: a two-function string task [@mock2026vibe, p. 12] vs 46 multi-requirement web apps.
  - Backbone: GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 [@mock2026vibe, p. 17] vs older or smaller backbones such as GPT-4o and Qwen2.5 [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 5].
  - Product: MetaGPT X web interface vs the open-source framework.
  - Evaluation: 12 runs pooled vs 46 projects x 3 runs.
- **Possible explanation** [I]: framework value depends on the backbone and the task scale. mock2026vibe's agentic advantage is confounded with the newer model generation.

### C7. Security of generated code: pan2026functional vs zhao2025vibe
- **Side A** [V]: Reference-normalised security averages 87.40% and is the strongest non-functional dimension [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
- **Side B** [V]: 79.3% of the functionally correct solutions of the best agent fail targeted security tests, and SecPass is only 3.8–12.9% [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
- **Differences**: pan2026functional counts high-risk static findings relative to the reference, and the score can reward incomplete code. zhao2025vibe runs 3.5 targeted security tests per task for a known historical CWE [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5]. The tasks also differ: whole-repository generation vs security-sensitive feature patches.
- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two instruments measure different things, a static absence of flagged patterns vs exploit-relevant behaviour. "Secure" cannot be compared across them.

### C8. More code or less code? Rebuilds are smaller, but assisted development adds code
- **Side A** [V]: Reconstructions are much smaller than their references. In bai2026recreationworld they are 89.4% smaller with 92.3% fewer files (4 of 10 models; desktop and Android only) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15]. In yang2026programbench they are shorter (median 1,173 vs 3,068 lines) and use fewer files [@yang2026programbench, p. 9].
- **Side B** [V]:
  - Cursor adoption raises lines added by +281.3% in month 1 [@he2026speed, p. 8].
  - AI-assisted Task 1 code produced outliers of up to 10,788 lines [@borg2026echoes, p. 30].
  - In MetaGPT apps, architectural smell counts track code size (ρ = 0.94) [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
  - The visual-fidelity leader writes 1,441 LoC vs 668 for GPT-5 [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
- **Differences**: rebuilds from scratch scored against a behavioural oracle of a mature original, vs incremental additions to existing projects or apps generated from a spec.
- **Possible explanation** [I]: reconstructions under-implement the original, which is consistent with low full-pass rates. Assisted development adds volume. Size therefore carries opposite signals in the two settings, and size-driven quality metrics (smell counts, totals) must be normalised before comparison.

### C9. Apparent disagreements that come from different constructs (do not pool)
- **"Vibe coding" means different things** [V]:
  - fawzy2026vibe: natural-language prompting plus re-prompting with minimal review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1].
  - asdaque2026novice: a supervised agent workflow, operationalised as opening agentic PRs [@asdaque2026novice, p. 1]. Its authors warn that the findings may not hold under a broader definition [@asdaque2026novice, p. 4].
  - mock2026vibe: human-written TDD tests plus scripted prompts that participants could not modify [@mock2026vibe, p. 15].
  - he2026speed: Cursor configuration files committed to a repository (intent-to-treat) [@he2026speed, p. 4].
  - ehsani2026faster: a driver of fast-integration debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 17].
  - [I] These are different interventions. Their results should not be pooled as "effects of vibe coding".
- **Fidelity scores are not comparable** [V]:
  - 58.06% average of programmatic and VLM channels [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
  - 36.35 Final Score (0.7 IFS + 0.3 VFS) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
  - 49.15% cumulative workflows [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11].
  - 53.75% Req.Acc with `data-testid` anchors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
  - 27.8% UI-agent accuracy with half credit for PARTIAL [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
  - 61.77% workflows passing at ≥90% of substeps [@tran2026vibe, p. 6].
  - 0% resolved / 3% almost [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
  - [I] Each figure uses a different oracle, input, application type and model generation. Do not rank across them.

### C10. Same model family builds or judges the benchmark and is evaluated (possible bias; untested)
- **Overlap and the same family wins** [V]:
  - yang2026programbench: Claude Sonnet 4.5 wrote the tests [@yang2026programbench, p. 3], and Claude models top the leaderboard [@yang2026programbench, p. 31].
  - tran2026vibe: GPT-5 drafted the specs [@tran2026vibe, p. 3], and GPT-5.3-Codex ranks first [@tran2026vibe, p. 6]. The canonical judge is Claude Sonnet 4.5 [@tran2026vibe, p. 4].
  - kim2026programdistill: GPT-5.6 Sol builds the tasks [@kim2026programdistill, p. 2], GPT-6 Astra ranks first [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8], and GPT-6 Astra also classifies the failures [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
  - zhao2025vibe: Claude 4 Sonnet runs the environment-building agent [@zhao2025vibe, p. 17], and SWE-agent constructs the tasks [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4]. The best setting is SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7].
- **Overlap without a visible advantage** [V]:
  - liu2026benchmarking: GPT-4o built the annotations and is evaluated [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 13]; the best backbone is Claude-Haiku.
  - lu2025webgen: GPT-4o wrote the test cases and scored low [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
  - bai2026recreationworld: the Qwen3.7-Plus judge is the lowest-scoring model (average 9.15) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
  - chen2025iwr: the Gemini-2.5-Pro judge ranks mid-table [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
  - wu2026looks: the judge is Gemini 2.5 Pro, Opus leads [@wu2026looks, p. 13], and the authors report no self-preference [A].
- [I] No paper tests construction-model or judge-model self-preference directly. The pattern is a validity threat, not a demonstrated bias.

## Agreements / converging evidence

- **G-A1. Whole-application functional fidelity is far from complete** [V]. Every benchmark agrees:
  - Full behavioural equivalence: 2.8% of apps [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] and 0 of 200 programs [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
  - Best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates: 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6].
  - Lower still in some benchmarks: IFS <25 [@chen2025iwr, p. 8], <45% [@pan2026functional, p. 5], 27.8% [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The direction is consistent across 8 independent benchmarks, but 5 of them are preprints and most use single runs.
- **G-A2. Behaviour and interaction are harder than static structure** [V]:
  - Structure beats actions [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
  - Static tasks score higher than interactive ones [@chen2025iwr, p. 16].
  - Interactive parts score lower than full pages [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
  - UI plus logic is harder than logic alone [@kim2026programdistill, p. 38].
  - "Click has no effect" is the largest navigation failure category (48.4%) [@wu2026looks, p. 8].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**, with the measurement caveat in C5.
- **G-A3. Fidelity falls as dependency depth, size or complexity rise** [V]: [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @tran2026vibe, p. 6; @zhao2025vibe, p. 14]. Strength [I]: **moderate**.
- **G-A4. Functional correctness and other quality dimensions diverge** [V]:
  - Best static quality but lowest Pass@1 [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
  - Correct but insecure [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
  - Equal functional scores but very different non-functional scores [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
  - The visual leader is not the maintainability leader [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
  - Authors state that passing functional tests does not imply maintainable code [A] [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The pattern is consistent, but each study measures a different second dimension.
- **G-A5. Rebuilt code is structurally simpler and more monolithic than the original** [V]: [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on 2 preprints, selected subsets and size proxies only.
- **G-A6. Code quality and maintainability are rarely measured in fidelity benchmarks**:
  - Not measured at all [V]: [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5; @kim2026programdistill, p. 14].
  - Explicitly left out [A]: [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
  - Measured only by proxies [V]: size and structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], LoC/reuse proxies [@wu2026looks, p. 4], a single MI index [@pan2026functional, p. 3], Likert ratings [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
  - Strength [I]: **strong** as a description of the field (verified absences across 12+ papers).
- **G-A7. LLM judges must be validated per judge model** [V]:
  - Judge–human agreement ranges from 36.1% to 86.4% depending on the evaluator model [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
  - 86–94% raw agreement on 3 settings [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
  - τ = 0.716 on 55 author-labelled scenarios [@wu2026looks, p. 13].
  - ρ = 0.65, tuned in-sample [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].
  - Low human inter-annotator κ (0.26–0.46) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 16].
  - Strength [I]: **moderate**.
- **G-A8. Practitioners perceive vibe-coded output as fast but flawed** [V]: [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8]. This converges with LLM-linked code and design debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16] and with higher review burden for novice agent users [@asdaque2026novice, p. 3]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on perception and proxy evidence, not code measurement.

# Methodology comparison: AI-assisted reverse engineering and vibe coding (functional fidelity, code quality, maintainability)

Project: 2026-11-11-ai-reverse-engineering-vibe-coding · Date: 2026-11-12 · Basis: 23 complete, full-text, critically reviewed analyses (`papers/*/analysis.md`) and `evidence-matrix.md`.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Seven papers are preprints (not peer-reviewed): bai2026recreationworld, chen2025iwr, kim2026programdistill, mota2026comparing, pan2026functional, yang2026programbench, zhao2025vibe. They are marked † below and carry less weight.

Terms used:
- An *oracle* is the reference that decides whether an output is correct, such as a test suite or a human judge.
- *Functional fidelity* means how closely a rebuilt app behaves like the original.
- An *LLM judge* is a language model used to score outputs in place of humans.

## 1. Overview table

All cells are [V] from the analyses unless marked otherwise. "n.r." = not reported.

| Paper | Design | Data / sample (N) | Setup | Metrics | Baselines | Statistical testing | Reproducibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| asdaque2026novice [@asdaque2026novice, p. 2] | MSR repository mining (5-page paper) | 22,953 agentic PRs from 1,719 users, AIDev, repos >100 stars | Low- vs high-experience split by commits / account age | Commits and files per PR, acceptance, time to merge, review comments | High-experience users; no non-AI PRs | Mann-Whitney, Chi-square, Benjamini-Hochberg; no effect sizes or CIs; test unit unclear [@asdaque2026novice, p. 4] | Public dataset + replication package [@asdaque2026novice, p. 5] |
| bai2026recreationworld† [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7] | Benchmark + SFT transfer | 250 apps (50 per platform: Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android, Web) x 10 models; rollouts n.r. (probably 1) | Isolated VMs; Codex or Claude Code scaffolds (model and scaffold confounded) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 28] | Programmatic accessibility/DOM tests + VLM assertions; LOC, files, largest-file share | Model vs model | No CIs or tests on main scores; bootstrap CIs on secondary analyses [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 12] | Release claimed [A] [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 27]; proprietary models; COI not declared [I] |
| borg2026echoes [@borg2026echoes, p. 24] | Preregistered 2-phase experiment; Phase 2 RCT | 151 professionals; Phase 1 n=76, Phase 2 n=75 (128 planned); 2 KLoC Java app | Second developer evolves AI-assisted or non-AI code without AI | Completion time, CodeScene CodeHealth (customised), JaCoCo coverage, perceived productivity | Non-AI code (control) | Wilcoxon/Welch, Cliff's δ / Cohen's d, bootstrap, Bayesian; no multiple-testing correction [@borg2026echoes, p. 19] | Zenodo + GitHub [@borg2026echoes, p. 74]; COI declared [@borg2026echoes, p. 75] |
| chen2025iwr† [@chen2025iwr, p. 6] | Benchmark | 113 video tasks from 100 websites x 28 LVLMs; runs n.r. | Video (≤64 frames) + assets → one HTML file; agent judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro) | IFS (action replay + assertions), VFS (OCR+DINO+MLLM), Final = 0.7 IFS + 0.3 VFS | Model vs model | None; weights tuned in-sample on 60 human-rated cases (ρ 0.57/0.65) [@chen2025iwr, p. 17] | Release promised [A] [@chen2025iwr, p. 1] |
| ehsani2026faster [@ehsani2026faster, p. 1] | Multivocal literature review | 31 peer-reviewed + 73 grey sources (to Jan 2026) | Dual extraction; κ 0.93 formal [@ehsani2026faster, p. 13] | Mention counts per debt type, tool, metric | Grey vs formal | None (descriptive) | figshare supplement [@ehsani2026faster, p. 4] |
| fawzy2026vibe [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 5] | Grey-literature review, thematic analysis | 101 sources, 518 coded units | Mainly single coder; subset cross-check [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 4] | Theme frequencies (quotes, not people) | None | None; no agreement statistic | Zenodo package [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 10] |
| he2026speed [@he2026speed, p. 4] | Staggered DiD + dynamic-panel GMM | 806 Cursor-adopting repos + 1,172–1,380 matched controls; 21,699 repo-months | Monthly panel Jan 2024–Aug 2025 | Commits, lines added; SonarQube warnings, cognitive complexity, duplication | Matched non-adopters (may use other AI) | ATT + SEs, pre-trend tests, Sargan/AR; estimator-sensitive [@he2026speed, p. 16] | Zenodo [@he2026speed, p. 11]; SonarQube version n.r. |
| kim2026programdistill† [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8] | Benchmark (LLM-built) | 300 partial tasks x 9 models; full rebuild 12 apps x 3 models = 36 runs | Browser CLI to a live reference; text observations only | Trace-replay binary and chain scores; atomic and cumulative recovery | Model vs model; no human baseline | None (means only) | Not yet released [A] [@kim2026programdistill, p. 1] |
| liu2026benchmarking [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 3] | Benchmark from existing apps | 46 web apps, 244 requirements, 703 BDD tests; 6 frameworks x 6 LLMs x 3 runs | Requirements + `data-testid` anchors in prompt [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 16] | Req.Acc, Test.Acc, cost, time | Vanilla LLM | Mean ± SD; no tests [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6] | Code + data released [A] [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 9] |
| lu2025webgen [@lu2025webgen, p. 5] | Benchmark + SFT | 101 instructions, 647 test cases x 16 settings; single run | Bolt.diy / OpenHands / Aider | UI-agent accuracy (half credit for PARTIAL), appearance 1–5 | Frameworks and models; no human baseline | None ("No" to error bars) [@lu2025webgen, p. 40] | Code, data, weights [A] [@lu2025webgen, p. 1] |
| mock2026vibe [@mock2026vibe, p. 16] | Static-group comparison + exploratory agent runs | 9 solo + 7 collaborative professionals; 3 fully-automated + 12 agentic runs; 2 small Python tasks | GPT-3.5 for humans vs GPT-5/Claude Sonnet 4 for agentic [@mock2026vibe, p. 17] | Baseline-test pass rate, McCabe, coverage, time | Solo human coding | KW, one-tailed MWU, Cliff's δ, Holm [@mock2026vibe, p. 10] | GitHub package [@mock2026vibe, p. 43] |
| molison2025llm [@molison2025llm, p. 4] | Comparative static analysis | APPS; GPT-4o zero/few/fine-tuned vs humans; N per group n.r.; Pass@1 on 15 per approach | SonarQube default profile [@molison2025llm, p. 5] | Bugs, smells, severity, fix effort, Pass@1 | APPS human solutions | ORs, MWU + Cliff's δ; no CIs or correction [@molison2025llm, p. 8] | Zenodo [@molison2025llm, p. 11] |
| mota2026comparing† [@mota2026comparing, p. 2] | Exploratory static analysis | 9 apps (Lovable, v0, Replit x 3), one prompt | Free tiers, May 2026 | SonarQube issues, severity, effort, duplication, per KLOC | Tools vs each other; no human or functional check | None (descriptive) [@mota2026comparing, p. 6] | Code + reports shared [@mota2026comparing, p. 6] |
| pan2026functional† [@pan2026functional, p. 2] | Benchmark | 38 Python repos x 16 LLMs x 3 runs; ~11 functional tests per task [@pan2026functional, p. 5] | Zero-shot single-pass repository generation | Functional pass rate; reference-normalised MI, security, robustness, efficiency, resource | Model vs model; reference as normalisation anchor | None; reruns + rank robustness [@pan2026functional, p. 10] | GitHub [A] [@pan2026functional, p. 11] |
| si2025benchmarking [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3] | Benchmark | 484 webpages (+80 HARD); human eval on 100 pages x 5 annotators | Screenshot → single HTML; greedy decoding | Block-Match, Text, Position, Color, CLIP; human win/tie/lose | MLLMs and prompts | Logistic regression validation (79.9%); no model tests [@si2025benchmarking, p. 7] | Release claimed, no URL [@si2025benchmarking, p. 10] |
| tran2026vibe [@tran2026vibe, p. 3] | Benchmark | 50 test apps (964 workflows total) x 16 models; 1 generation each [I] | OpenHands-based harness, React/Vite + Supabase | Workflow pass (≥90% substeps) by LLM browser agent; cost; latency | Model vs model | Mean ± SE across apps; variance panel; human alignment [@tran2026vibe, p. 8] | Harness + trajectories released [A] [@tran2026vibe, p. 11] |
| wu2026looks [@wu2026looks, p. 3] | Benchmark | 29 apps, 309 screens, 701 nav specs x 6 models = 174 single runs | Screenshots + page-relationship description → React/TS | Build, NavPass, Borda VLM visual, LoC/reuse/dead-component proxies | Model vs model | Wilson CIs for failure sample only [@wu2026looks, p. 8] | Repo + one-command replay [A] [@wu2026looks, p. 10] |
| xiao2025benchmarking [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 3] | Benchmark + user study | 127 pages / 374 interactions x 6 MLLMs x 3 prompts; user study 4 people | Before/after interaction screenshots → one HTML file | CLIP, SSIM, text, Implement Rate; human Usability Rate | Direct prompting | None; human–metric "consistency" claimed only [A] [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6] | GitHub [A] [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 1] |
| xiong2026propgen [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7] | Tool + evaluation | 12 Android apps; 985 properties; single run | GPT-5.2 runtime exploration + property synthesis | Functionality / property validity, refinement, new bugs | DroidAgent, naive LLM, 4 bug detectors | Cohen's κ 0.81–0.91 only | Zenodo [A] [@xiong2026propgen, p. 13] |
| yang2026programbench† [@yang2026programbench, p. 4] | Benchmark | 200 programs x 9 models = 1,800 runs; 248,853 tests | Execute-only binary + docs, no internet, mini-SWE-agent [@yang2026programbench, p. 5] | % resolved, % almost, % tests passed, structure stats | Model vs model; native test suites for coverage | None; Fleiss' κ for cheating judges [@yang2026programbench, p. 17] | Open-sourced [A] [@yang2026programbench, p. 2] |
| zhao2025vibe† [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6] | Benchmark | 186 tasks from 100 Python repos x 12 agent settings; single pass@1 | Agents re-implement a masked feature | FuncPass, SecPass, CWE P/R/F1 | Settings vs each other | None [@zhao2025vibe, p. 8] | GitHub [A] [@zhao2025vibe, p. 1] |
| zhou2025declarui [@zhou2025declarui, p. 6] | Technique + comparison + user study | 50 apps (250 pages); ablation 13 apps; 5 developers x 12 apps | CV + MLLM page-transition graph + compile/navigation refinement; human graph correction [@zhou2025declarui, p. 4] | CLIP, SSIM, PCR, CSR, ACIC, AMCT; Likert readability and maintainability | Raw GPT-4o / Claude-3.5 | MWU on non-independent ratings only [@zhou2025declarui, p. 10] | No code or data link (n.r.) |
| zhu2026understanding [@zhu2026understanding, p. 4] | Exploratory static analysis (2 experiments) | Exp I: 90 problems x 5 LLMs x 2 prompts + 90 human; Exp II: ~20 MetaGPT apps [I] | PyExamine smell detection | Code / structural / architectural smell counts, LoC | Human solutions (Exp I) | Exp I none; Exp II Spearman / KW without correction [@zhu2026understanding, p. 9] | Zenodo [@zhu2026understanding, p. 10] |

## 2. Approach families

**F1. Visual UI-to-code (screenshot or design → code):** si2025benchmarking, xiao2025benchmarking, zhou2025declarui, wu2026looks.
- Strengths [I]: real webpages and apps as references [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2; @wu2026looks, p. 3]. Each paper also adds some reliability check:
  - visual metrics partly validated against humans [@si2025benchmarking, p. 7];
  - a human-calibrated VLM judge with an anchor [@wu2026looks, p. 13];
  - navigation measured with app exploration [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
- Weaknesses [I]:
  - Fidelity is mostly visual. si2025benchmarking strips JavaScript [@si2025benchmarking, p. 13].
  - Interaction coverage is shallow: navigation edges only [@wu2026looks, p. 5], or element presence as "Implement Rate" [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 4].
  - Structural priors are given as input: a page-relationship description [@wu2026looks, p. 3] or a human-corrected page-transition graph [@zhou2025declarui, p. 4].
  - Code quality is unmeasured or measured by proxies or Likert ratings.

**F2. Behaviour-observed reconstruction (video, live reference or executable → app):** chen2025iwr†, bai2026recreationworld†, kim2026programdistill†, yang2026programbench†.
- This family is the closest match to "AI-assisted reverse engineering" [I].
- Strengths [I]: implementation-agnostic behavioural oracles [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 4; @yang2026programbench, p. 5; @kim2026programdistill, p. 4]. The papers also use:
  - leakage and isolation controls [@yang2026programbench, p. 18; @kim2026programdistill, p. 10; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 9];
  - oracle-quality audits: coverage [@yang2026programbench, p. 7] and interaction-outcome share [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 9].
- Weaknesses [I]:
  - All four are preprints, and all use single runs.
  - Same-family builders appear in yang2026programbench and kim2026programdistill (see Contradiction C10 in the evidence matrix).
  - Code quality is measured only through size and structure proxies [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9] or not at all [@kim2026programdistill, p. 6].
  - Oracles are coupled to the original's selectors in kim2026programdistill [@kim2026programdistill, p. 35].

**F3. Specification-to-app benchmarks with executable oracles:** liu2026benchmarking, lu2025webgen, tran2026vibe, pan2026functional†, zhao2025vibe†.
- Strengths [I]: requirement-level executable tests. Several papers check their oracles:
  - expert test audits [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 14];
  - judge–human alignment [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @lu2025webgen, p. 9];
  - reference-validated tests [@pan2026functional, p. 2];
  - upstream human tests with no LLM judge [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5].
- Two papers start from existing apps, which brings them close to reconstruction: liu2026benchmarking and pan2026functional [I].
- Weaknesses [I]:
  - The input is a written specification, not observed behaviour.
  - LLM judges and LLM-drafted tests are used (tran2026vibe, lu2025webgen).
  - Oracles are thin: about 11 tests per task [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
  - Only pan2026functional measures maintainability, through one MI proxy [@pan2026functional, p. 3].

**F4. Code-quality studies of LLM or vibe-coded code (static analysis):** molison2025llm, mota2026comparing†, zhu2026understanding, he2026speed (plus the non-functional arm of pan2026functional).
- Strengths [I]: established tools (SonarQube, PyExamine), and one quasi-causal design at scale [@he2026speed, p. 7].
- Weaknesses [I]:
  - The instruments disagree with each other (C3).
  - Counts are often not normalised by size [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
  - Functional correctness is not checked [@mota2026comparing, p. 2], or checked only on 15 samples [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
  - Human baselines are weak (competitive-programming submissions) [@molison2025llm, p. 9].
  - Tasks are algorithmic snippets, not applications (molison2025llm, zhu2026understanding Exp I).

**F5. Human-centred and workflow studies:** borg2026echoes (RCT), mock2026vibe (experiment), asdaque2026novice (mining), fawzy2026vibe (grey review), ehsani2026faster (multivocal review).
- Strengths [I]:
  - The only randomised maintainability evidence, a hand-off evolution design [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
  - Real developers [@mock2026vibe, p. 16].
  - Practitioner definitions of vibe coding [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1].
  - A technical-debt taxonomy [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16].
- Weaknesses [I]:
  - Small or underpowered samples [@borg2026echoes, p. 19; @mock2026vibe, p. 13].
  - Model-generation confound [@mock2026vibe, p. 17].
  - Perception or proxy outcomes [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8; @asdaque2026novice, p. 2].
  - Reviews rely heavily on grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16].
  - None studies reconstruction.

**F6. Behavioural-specification recovery from running apps:** xiong2026propgen.
- Strengths [I]: runtime-grounded property inference with independent annotators (κ 0.81–0.91) [@xiong2026propgen, p. 7]. It is a candidate oracle generator for fidelity testing.
- Weaknesses [I]: 12 apps, single run, author-tool overlap in the baselines, and it generates no code.

## 3. Comparable results

**Rule:** numbers are compared only between papers that share the dataset, the metric and the setup. **No pair of papers in this corpus meets all three.** So all cross-paper statements below are directional, not quantitative.

| Pair (closest candidates) | What they share | Why the numbers are not comparable |
|---|---|---|
| si2025benchmarking vs xiao2025benchmarking | C4 validation-set pages, CLIP [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 2] | Static pages vs interaction regions; different subsets and models; different extra metrics |
| zhou2025declarui vs wu2026looks | Multi-screen mobile apps rebuilt from screenshots | PCR (graph edges, scored manually) vs NavPass (Playwright tests); native frameworks vs a React web proxy; different structural inputs |
| bai2026recreationworld vs chen2025iwr | A functional channel plus a visual channel | Accessibility tests + VLM assertions vs action replay + OCR/DINO/MLLM; VFS only over reached checkpoints [@chen2025iwr, p. 7] |
| lu2025webgen vs tran2026vibe | NL spec → web app; LLM browser judge | Atomic test cases with half credit vs workflows passing at ≥90% of substeps; different model generations |
| liu2026benchmarking vs pan2026functional | Rebuild of existing open-source apps against reference-validated tests | Web BDD via Selenium with `data-testid` anchors vs Python pytest on public APIs; different models |
| molison2025llm vs zhu2026understanding (Exp I) | Competitive-programming problems vs human solutions | APPS + SonarQube vs CodeContests + PyExamine; different models |
| he2026speed vs mota2026comparing | SonarQube issue measures | Change in repository-month totals vs per-KLOC issues in 9 generated apps |
| pan2026functional vs zhao2025vibe | Python repositories, test-based correctness, a "security" score | Whole-repo generation + static findings vs feature patch + targeted security tests (C7) |

Headline functional-fidelity figures, listed for orientation only. They are **not comparable** because each has a different oracle, input and app type [I]:

| Paper | Input → output | Oracle | Best reported |
|---|---|---|---|
| yang2026programbench† | Executable + docs → CLI program | ~770 behavioural tests per task (median) | 0% resolved; ≥95% of tests on 3% of tasks [@yang2026programbench, p. 6] |
| bai2026recreationworld† | Running app → app (5 platforms) | Accessibility/DOM tests + VLM | 58.06% average; 2.8% full programmatic pass [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] |
| kim2026programdistill† | Live web app → web app | Browser-trace replay | 49.15% cumulative workflows (3 models, 12 apps) [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11] |
| chen2025iwr† | Interaction video → single HTML | Agent replay + MLLM assertions | Final 36.35, IFS 24.39 [@chen2025iwr, p. 8] |
| liu2026benchmarking | Requirements from existing apps → web app | BDD/Selenium tests | 53.75% Req.Acc [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6] |
| tran2026vibe | NL spec → full-stack web app | LLM browser workflows | 61.77% workflows [@tran2026vibe, p. 6] |
| lu2025webgen | NL instruction → website | UI-agent test cases | 27.8% accuracy [@lu2025webgen, p. 8] |
| pan2026functional† | Requirements → Python repo | pytest suites | <45% pass rate [@pan2026functional, p. 5] |
| zhao2025vibe† | Feature description → patch | Upstream functional tests | 57.0% FuncPass [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7] |
| wu2026looks | Screenshots + navigation map → React app | Playwright navigation | 92% NavPass [@wu2026looks, p. 7] |
| zhou2025declarui | Screenshots/designs → mobile UI | Manual graph-edge coverage | 96.8% PCR [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9] |

Within-paper model rankings are comparable, but single runs make near-ties uninterpretable:
- [V] tran2026vibe shows that generation variance dominates evaluator variance (73.5–92.5%) [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
- [I] Rank gaps of a few points in yang2026programbench, wu2026looks, lu2025webgen and zhao2025vibe cannot be separated from noise.

## 4. Contradictions

The full entries with both sides, differences and [I] explanations are in `evidence-matrix.md` → "Contradictions". Summary:

1. **C1 Maintainability harm.** Project-level warnings and complexity rise after Cursor adoption [@he2026speed, p. 7], but a second developer's effort and CodeHealth show no significant difference [@borg2026echoes, p. 33; @borg2026echoes, p. 38]. Tools, units, scale and time differ, and the he2026speed effect depends on the estimator [@he2026speed, p. 16].
2. **C2 Static issues.** LLM code has fewer SonarQube bugs than APPS humans [@molison2025llm, p. 8], vs +30% repository warnings [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The units and baselines differ, so the results are not comparable.
3. **C3 Instrument choice.** PyExamine is chosen over SonarQube's "superficial linting" [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2]. Technical-debt tools disagree [@ehsani2026faster, p. 5].
4. **C4 Iterative feedback.**
   - It hurts non-functional quality without functional gain [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
   - It correlates with or enables better outcomes elsewhere [@tran2026vibe, p. 7; @zhou2025declarui, p. 10; @wu2026looks, p. 12].
   - The studies differ in feedback type, outcome and design (intervention vs correlation).
5. **C5 Looks vs behaves.** chen2025iwr and bai2026recreationworld are only directionally consistent. VFS > IFS is partly built into chen2025iwr's metrics [@chen2025iwr, p. 7]. In bai2026recreationworld the visual channel is below the programmatic one for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
6. **C6 MetaGPT.** It nearly always fails in liu2026benchmarking [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6] but leads on tiny tasks with newer models in mock2026vibe [@mock2026vibe, p. 41].
7. **C7 Security.** 87.40% static security [@pan2026functional, p. 6] vs 79.3% of correct solutions failing targeted tests [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
8. **C8 Code volume.** Rebuilds are smaller than the originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], while assisted development adds code [@he2026speed, p. 8; @borg2026echoes, p. 30].
9. **C9 Construct differences.** "Vibe coding" is defined differently in [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1; @asdaque2026novice, p. 1; @mock2026vibe, p. 15; @he2026speed, p. 4; @ehsani2026faster, p. 17], so these results must not be pooled. The fidelity scores of kim2026programdistill, liu2026benchmarking, lu2025webgen, bai2026recreationworld and chen2025iwr use different oracles and are not comparable.
10. **C10 Same-family construction or judging.** The same model family builds or judges the benchmark and then wins in yang2026programbench, tran2026vibe, kim2026programdistill and zhao2025vibe. There is overlap without a visible advantage in liu2026benchmarking, lu2025webgen, bai2026recreationworld, chen2025iwr and wu2026looks. This is untested everywhere [I].

## 5. Methodological weaknesses across the field

Counts are our tally over the analyses [I]. Each pattern is verified in the cited papers.

1. **Single runs, no variance, no significance tests.**
   - Main results come from one run or generation per cell, or the number of runs is not reported. Examples: [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11; @chen2025iwr, p. 8; @kim2026programdistill, p. 12; @lu2025webgen, p. 40; @wu2026looks, p. 9; @yang2026programbench, p. 10; @zhao2025vibe, p. 6; @xiong2026propgen, p. 8].
   - Studies that repeat runs: liu2026benchmarking (3 runs) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 5], pan2026functional (3 runs + 5 reruns) [@pan2026functional, p. 5], and tran2026vibe's 6-app variance panel [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
   - No benchmark paper tests model differences for significance. Where measured, run-to-run variance is large: generation SE up to 5 pp [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
2. **Unvalidated or same-family oracles and judges.**
   - Many papers use LLM-drafted tests, LLM-built tasks or LLM judges, often from the evaluated families (C10).
   - Judge validation uses raw percent agreement without chance correction [@tran2026vibe, p. 9; @lu2025webgen, p. 9], small or author-labelled panels [@wu2026looks, p. 13], or in-sample calibration [@chen2025iwr, p. 17; @si2025benchmarking, p. 17].
   - Some automatic metrics are only declared "consistent" with humans [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
3. **Contamination handling is uneven.**
   - Reference apps and programs are popular public projects in most benchmarks.
   - Explicit controls appear in only a few: an overlap audit [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 18], no internet plus a language ablation [@yang2026programbench, p. 6], BLEU against the original [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5], post-cutoff builds [@xiong2026propgen, p. 11], and keeping task code out of public repositories [@borg2026echoes, p. 66].
   - pan2026functional acknowledges exposure [@pan2026functional, p. 2], and its example prompt names the original project [@pan2026functional, p. 3].
   - No contamination discussion was found for chen2025iwr, kim2026programdistill, liu2026benchmarking, si2025benchmarking, wu2026looks, zhao2025vibe, molison2025llm or zhu2026understanding (per their analyses) [I].
4. **Code quality and maintainability are absent or measured by unvalidated proxies.**
   - The proxies used are size and structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], LoC/reuse/dead-component counts [@wu2026looks, p. 4], a single MI index [@pan2026functional, p. 3], Likert ratings [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7], and raw smell counts not normalised by size [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
   - No reconstruction benchmark combines a behavioural oracle with a validated maintainability measure or a hand-off maintenance task like the one in borg2026echoes [@borg2026echoes, p. 13] [I].
5. **Oracle coupling and incompleteness make fidelity scores incomparable.**
   - Tests are tied to the original's identifiers: `data-testid` anchors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 16] and selectors [@kim2026programdistill, p. 35].
   - Structural priors are given as input [@wu2026looks, p. 3; @zhou2025declarui, p. 4].
   - Suites are thin: about 11 tests per task [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
   - Finite suites can only give a lower bound [@yang2026programbench, p. 12; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 22].
   - Metrics are partly circular: navigation is scored against the method's own input graph [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7], and VFS uses a different denominator [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
6. **Further recurring problems:**
   - No human-developer baseline in any reconstruction or generation benchmark [@yang2026programbench, p. 20; @tran2026vibe, p. 5; @lu2025webgen, p. 7].
   - Small human samples [@mock2026vibe, p. 16; @zhou2025declarui, p. 10; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 11].
   - Underpowered RCT [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
   - Internal numeric inconsistencies, flagged in the analyses of borg2026echoes, he2026speed, liu2026benchmarking, molison2025llm, wu2026looks, xiao2025benchmarking, yang2026programbench and zhou2025declarui (see each paper's §9) [I].
   - Construct heterogeneity of "vibe coding" (C9).
   - Almost exclusively web, Python or CLI targets. Only bai2026recreationworld covers native desktop and Android [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 7]; mobile work uses a web proxy [@wu2026looks, p. 9] or UI-only code [@zhou2025declarui, p. 2].

## 6. What this means for our RQs

**RQ1 (approaches and their relation to vibe coding).**
- Six approach families exist (§2). Inputs range from screenshots, designs, interaction videos and before/after interaction screenshots to live running references, executables plus docs, and natural-language specs [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4; @chen2025iwr, p. 5; @bai2026recreationworld, p. 3; @kim2026programdistill, p. 3; @yang2026programbench, p. 2; @tran2026vibe, p. 3] [V].
- Almost all evaluations run autonomous agents or single prompts. Practitioner vibe coding is human-steered natural-language prompting with little review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1], and that is studied only in small human experiments [@mock2026vibe, p. 15] or as a field proxy [@he2026speed, p. 4] [I].
- Evidence strength: **moderate**. The descriptive picture is consistent, but 7 of 23 papers are preprints and the field moves monthly.

**RQ2 (measuring functional fidelity and how well it is achieved).**
- Fidelity is measured by four oracle types [I]:
  - behavioural test replay (bai2026recreationworld, kim2026programdistill, yang2026programbench, liu2026benchmarking, pan2026functional, zhao2025vibe);
  - LLM or agent judges running natural-language tests (lu2025webgen, tran2026vibe, chen2025iwr);
  - visual similarity (si2025benchmarking, xiao2025benchmarking, wu2026looks, zhou2025declarui);
  - navigation graphs (wu2026looks, zhou2025declarui).
- Achieved fidelity is partial everywhere:
  - full equivalence is rare [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11; @yang2026programbench, p. 6];
  - the best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates are about 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6];
  - interaction logic lags static structure (G-A2).
- Evidence strength: **moderate** for "fidelity is far from complete and interaction is the bottleneck". **Weak** for any specific number or cross-benchmark ranking (C9, §3).

**RQ3 (code quality and maintainability vs human code).**
- The evidence is mixed and does not support a single answer.
  - Project-level warnings and complexity rise, but the result is estimator-sensitive and size-driven [@he2026speed, p. 7; @he2026speed, p. 16].
  - No short-term downstream maintainability harm was found in an RCT [@borg2026echoes, p. 38].
  - LLM code has fewer SonarQube bugs than a weak human baseline, with mixed smells [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
  - LLM code shows different smell types [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
  - Quality is platform-dependent [@mota2026comparing, p. 5].
  - Rebuilds are smaller and more monolithic than the originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9].
  - Practitioners perceive the code as "fast but flawed" [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8].
- No study measures validated maintainability of *reconstructed* applications against their originals [I].
- Evidence strength: **weak to moderate** (conflicting results, C1–C3).

**RQ4 (methodological strengths and weaknesses).**
- Strengths: implementation-agnostic behavioural oracles with leakage controls (F2), oracle audits (coverage, expert κ), judge–human alignment checks, and one preregistered RCT.
- Weaknesses: the six patterns in §5.
- Evidence strength: **strong** for missing variance and significance testing and for absent maintainability measurement (verified across 12+ papers). **Moderate** for judge, contamination and oracle-coupling problems.

**RQ5 (gaps and study design).**
- The convergent weak point is the missing joint evaluation of behavioural fidelity *and* validated maintainability for UI- or behaviour-based reconstruction [I]. The partial exceptions are pan2026functional (Python APIs, MI only), wu2026looks (proxies) and zhou2025declarui (Likert).
- Candidate gaps for the gap analyst are listed below. **None is claimed as a gap yet: each needs the novelty check in docs/research-standards.md §7.**
  1. Joint fidelity + maintainability evaluation of AI-reconstructed apps against their originals, using static quality with size normalisation and more than one tool, plus a hand-off maintenance task as in borg2026echoes.
  2. Human-steered vibe-coding reconstruction compared with autonomous agents. All benchmarks are autonomous; future-work statements: [@yang2026programbench, p. 12; @kim2026programdistill, p. 14].
  3. Contamination-controlled reconstruction targets, such as post-cutoff, obfuscated or private reference apps (uneven handling, §5.3).
  4. Judge and oracle independence: cross-family judges, chance-corrected agreement, and tests of builder- or judge-family self-preference (C10).
  5. Whether iterative feedback or self-testing improves fidelity *and* code quality together (C4).
  6. Validity of maintainability instruments for AI-generated code: SonarQube vs PyExamine vs CodeHealth vs MI (C3).
  7. Black-box oracles that are not coupled to the original's identifiers (§5.5).
  8. Native mobile and back-end-inclusive reconstruction.
- A design sketch [I]:
  - reference apps of known provenance (post-cutoff or private);
  - several vibe-coding tools and agents, plus a human-steered arm;
  - ≥3 runs per cell;
  - a behavioural oracle (trace replay or BDD, black-box selectors) plus a validated visual judge;
  - size-normalised static quality from two tools plus a second-developer change task;
  - cross-family judges with κ reporting and preregistered tests.
- Evidence strength: **weak** (pending novelty check).

# Methodology comparison: AI-assisted reverse engineering and vibe coding (functional fidelity, code quality, maintainability)

Project: 2026-11-11-ai-reverse-engineering-vibe-coding · Date: 2026-11-12 · Basis: 23 complete, full-text, critically reviewed analyses (`papers/*/analysis.md`) and `evidence-matrix.md`.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Seven papers are preprints (not peer-reviewed): bai2026recreationworld, chen2025iwr, kim2026programdistill, mota2026comparing, pan2026functional, yang2026programbench, zhao2025vibe. They are marked † below and carry less weight.

Terms used:
- An *oracle* is the reference that decides whether an output is correct, such as a test suite or a human judge.
- *Functional fidelity* means how closely a rebuilt app behaves like the original.
- An *LLM judge* is a language model used to score outputs in place of humans.

## 1. Overview table

All cells are [V] from the analyses unless marked otherwise. "n.r." = not reported.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
